utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Just before I warn the witness, Mr. Whiting, you're cross-examining. What are the chances of us finishing with this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Extremely high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Extremely high? I'm grateful to hear that. No explanation, thank you very much. Okay. Mr. Plejo, I warn you once again that you took -- you didn't take but you made a declaration in the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth. Okay? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On Wednesday, you testified that the two most common reasons for discipline in the Knin prison were failing to report and excessive force. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also testified that when the ICRC visited the prison, that almost all their comments had to do with the material side of things such as hygiene, and Mr. Milovancevic asked you, then, if that meant that hygiene was the greatest problem. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's clear from your testimony that the ICRC did not learn about these cases of excessive force, did it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said that they could directly talk with them, without any prison staff being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, please. If you could just listen to my question and focus on the question and just answer my question. It's clear that the ICRC did not learn about the cases of excessive force because the only things they told -- the only complaints that they related to you had to do with the material side of things, such as hygiene, so they didn't learn about the cases of excessive force; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what they told me, and I don't know what they were told, and I don't know whether they knew or didn't know. I presume that had there been such excessive force they would have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you told us that there were cases of excessive force. And wouldn't you expect, given what you saw and learned at the time, that had the ICRC heard about these cases of excessive force, it would have related that to you in their -- among their complaints, but that did not happen, did it? So from that, you could conclude that they did not in fact learn about the cases of excessive force; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to tell you now. I don't remember whether there were any such complaints on their part, but they could have known if the inmates had told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's not my question, sir. And on Wednesday, when you addressed this topic, on this topic you didn't say you had any difficulty remembering and you told us that the complaints had to do with the material side of things such as hygiene. So aren't you able to conclude -- aren't you able to conclude from what you observed and heard, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection to raise. This question can be put to representatives of the International Red Cross, not the witness. The witness has explained what was done and how it was done and how the International Committee of the Red Cross visited the detainees. My colleague should bring him the ICRC representatives and ask them this question rather than ask the witness what it was that they had learned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I accept 110 per cent, Mr. Milovancevic, that this question can be but to the representatives of the ICRC. My -- what I can't find in your objection is what's wrong with putting the question to this witness. You haven't told us -- you're telling us the person it could be put to. It doesn't mean that it can't be put to any other person. In fact -- in fact, this person cannot -- this question cannot be put to the ICRC. The ICRC will just be put -- you just ask them directly, were you told about the excessive use of force? You wouldn't be asking them whether they can conclude anything. I think this -- the question whether anything can be concluded is appropriate for this witness. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would also note that the ICRC has a policy of not testifying in cases. So in fact the question cannot be put to the ICRC but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not even the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir the objection has been overruled. So I'm going to put the question to you just again and if you please answer my question. Aren't you able to conclude from what you observed and what you learned from the ICRC what they did tell you about, what they didn't tell you about, that in fact they did not learn about these cases of excessive force?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they did or did not learn about it. What I described was what were -- what their most frequent complaints. It is quite possible that I might have instituted some disciplinary proceedings at their initiative and they were able to talk directly to all the detainees and to elicit whatever information they wanted. No one prevented that. Also, the inmates wrote letters and sent them to their respective homes via the ICRC and could tell them whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, again, on Wednesday, when you were asked this question, it's at transcript page 8738, you were asked on direct examination about the ICRC and you were asked what the comments were about and your answer was: "Almost all of them had to do with the material side of things. I had a hard time explaining to them that whatever difficulties we had in the prison concerning hygiene and some other things they were common to the population outside the prison." There is no mention in that answer or in any subsequent answers on this topic about complaints that the ICRC made about excessive force. Now, are you telling us today for the first time that in fact there may have been complaints about excessive force?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that almost all, not all of the complaints related to hygienic conditions, more shampoo, more soap and such improvements. And I told them please feel free to also bring such sanitation supplies yourself to them and they did occasionally, and cigarettes as well. Even we, the staff, were short of all such supplies but whether there were any such cases, I don't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the truth is that the ICRC did not learn about cases of excessive force because prisoners who had been beaten in that prison were hidden from the ICRC, isn't that the truth, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, they could not have been hidden because the Red Cross people came at least once a week and once they registered a person, the next week they would seek out that person and wanted to talk to him. It was impossible to hide anyone from the Red Cross, in other words. They actually would ask to see people according to a list which they had and they had lists of all the detainees in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about Nikola Kukavica. On the first day of your testimony, and this may, to be fair this may have been just simply an interpretation issue or a misspeaking but I just want to clear it up. On the first day of your testimony, at 8740 you said that he stayed for only two days as warden and then yesterday, at 8824, you said it was several months or two months. Now, in fact, it was several months that he stayed, correct, not just two days, as warden?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it says two days. I didn't say two days. I thought I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clear it up. If you could just answer the question, it was two to three months; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say off the cuff exactly, he was there for a while. I don't know the exact dates and I don't know whether the man stayed there for a month or two months. Now, after 15 years have passed, I cannot remember for how long Nikola Kukavica was prison warden but it was a short time. It couldn't have been a half year or a year. Whether it was 15 days or a month, I cannot know that after 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. If -- I'm going to ask if you -- I predicted to the Trial Chamber that we would finish with you today but if your answers are very long, it's going to be hard to do that and I'm sure you want to finish today. So I'm just going to ask if you could, please try to just answer the question and answer it as briefly as possible. Now, when Mr. Kukavica was the warden of the prison, he actually tried to impose some order in that prison, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man was doing his job. I don't know. I didn't control the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, he dismissed two guards, Djuro Banjeglav and Miroslav Orlovic because they had beaten some prisoners; isn't that right? Remember that, that he did that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I was also replaced. I had -- sorry, I had replaced, I had sent them away from work, I remember that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your memory is that you're the one who replaced them, not Mr. Kukavica?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, you reinstated them, didn't you? You let them have their jobs back.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I first suspended them and I believe that Orlovic was later dismissed altogether, that actually I wrote his dismissal decision myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's your memory?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Banjeglav was allowed to come back to the prison, wasn't he, he was allowed to resume his work as a guard, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was given his job back but I'm not quite sure. I'm not sure whether both were dismissed. There were several instances of dismissals. I'm not sure. But I believe only Orlovic was laid off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, your testimony on Wednesday was that frequently these guards would be suspended but then they would be reinstated because you claimed that you had a shortage of guards and that you needed to reinstate them. Isn't that in fact what happened to these two men? They were reinstated?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained a minute ago. I believe that one of them was reinstated and the other one was dismissed, and we were short of staff, it was very difficult to work, and there were few people available in that line of duty. Had we been able to recruit new staff, both would have been dismissed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they were disciplined because they had beaten prisoners; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes. Whether both of them, I don't know, but I'm quite certain as far as Orlovic is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Whiting, one moment before you proceed. They would be reinstated after suspension or after dismissal? Because my understanding that reinstatement is something that hams after a person is dismissed but suspension is merely keeping them away from work for a particular period, the work isn't lost. So I would like a clarification there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll seek to get the clarification from the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, what is your recollection about what happened with these two men? Were they suspended, were they dismissed, and then what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were suspended and I believe that only Orlovic was dismissed. When you show me the document yesterday, you could see next to his name it was indicated that he was suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that after that document was written, he was later suspended? I mean dismissed. He had been suspended first and then dismissed. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I'm saying. The first measure is suspension and that can be followed either by returning the person to work or by a total termination of the person's employment, dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, suspension -- a person is only suspended after a disciplinary proceeding, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warden can suspend him even before that, and then disciplinary proceedings can be instituted afterwards, but also disciplinary proceedings can be instituted beforehand. Both were possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you have any memory of what happened in this case, with these two men? Was there a disciplinary proceeding and then they were suspended? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were suspended immediately. I cannot remember right now. And then the disciplinary proceedings were instituted. After the disciplinary proceedings, I accepted the ruling of the disciplinary commission regarding Banjeglav and as for Orlovic, I did not accept that he only be find but I had him dismissed. I dismissed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was the disciplinary ruling with respect to Banjeglav that you accepted? What was the ruling?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I believe that the punishment was suspension for a period of time and there were some subsequent deductions from his salary for the following three or six months, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And again, he had beaten prisoners, hadn't he? That's why he was disciplined, for beating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I would have to consult the case file. I cannot know from memory. Maybe he was an accomplice. Maybe he was the chief of the guards' shift and allowed something to happen. I would really have to consult the file to be able to tell you exactly what had happened but I cannot from memory now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But is it fair to say that it had -- whatever his role was, it involved the use of excessive force? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's true, isn't it? That is in fact what happened, isn't it? Not just possible, that is in fact what happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you I don't know from memory. It was not perhaps his excessive use of force. It may have been the chief of the shift of guards. I don't know what his actual involvement was. Probably it was something lesser than that of Orlovic because this other person was dismissed and he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please listen to my question. My question was, whatever his role was, whether he was an accomplice or chief or bigger role or lesser role, he was disciplined for an event involving excessive force; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to another topic. You testified on Wednesday that the Courts made the decisions on whether someone would be placed in the premises of the Knin district prison. It's at 8749. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's not true for prisoners of war or that was not -- that was not true for prisoners of war, was it? That decision could be made by the army or the police; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was mainly the Courts that adopted that, but if the minister sent me a decision stating that I had to admit someone according to a decision of the army or the police, I will have also to admit such prisoners, but they all had some written decisions to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's just be perfectly clear about your answer here. The army and the police had the power, had the authority, to put somebody, a prisoner of war, in the Knin district prison without any order from a court; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have to take the person involved before the district court in Knin and the district court would then pass a decision on the detention of such persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you but can we just get clarity? The minister referred to at page 10, line 25, which minister is this? Is this the Minister of Justice or the Minister of any other department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Minister of Justice, Your Honour. That is the department concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the district court that you have referred to, the district court in Knin, that was a civilian court; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what authority would a civilian court have to order a war prisoner be held?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact, in fact, the army and the police had that authority, didn't they? And they are the one who would request that prisoners be held in the Knin district prison, prisoners of war, that is?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know who did the requesting or the deciding. I just acted upon decisions by courts. I could not admit to you to prison if you didn't have a relevant court's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at a document authored by you. It's Exhibit 908 and if we could look at page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. Do you remember looking at this report, sir, in your direct examination on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this was a report that was written by you on the 31st of December, 1994, and I draw your attention to that first paragraph there, and it says, "In view of the fact that the past period was a period of the state of war or imminent war threat, we were also admitting prisoners of war at the district prison in Knin." And here is the important sentence: "These persons were admitted on the basis of decisions issued by the Serbian army of Krajina and members of public security stations." Now, you wrote that sentence; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was true, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what you said a moment ago was incorrect, that the prisoners of war were admitted on -- only on the basis of court decisions. It says right here that they were admitted on the basis of decisions from the army and from the police; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said a while ago was true. You asked me about the period while I was warden. This here is two years later, when I was the keeper of the central records. So I also said that the minister could issue approval for prisoners of war to be admitted to the prison who were brought there by the army or the police, but also, as stated here, they also had to have a decision to that effect and I believe that I've said all this. Meaning, in this case, that probably the Minister of Justice and administration had approved that prisoners be admitted according to those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear. The practice that was being followed and that is -- at this time, when you were the records keeper, is the same practice that was being followed when you were the warden, wasn't it? The practice didn't change. It was the same. With respect to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was almost the same. It was almost the same but I said that the minister perhaps rendered a decision and we were interested in operating --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir there is no mention of a decision of the Minister of Justice in this report, is there? The only thing that's mentioned is decisions by the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in the prison we couldn't take anyone in without a decision. We took people in with a decision but a decision must have been rendered by those who issued decisions. It was the Ministry of Justice and Administration. It was the Courts who did such things and I wasn't that interested in it. I was interested in being covered, in having the appropriate papers for the action that is we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But let's just try to be clear about this. The police and the army could also -- you said you needed a decision in order to hold a prisoner. You could get a decision from the police and the army. They could give you a decision to hold a prisoner; right? As is reflected in this report.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police would bring in Serbs and criminals too so I -- I'm not quite sure how to explain this to you in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you certainly won't be able to explain it if you talk about something different than what I'm asking about. I'm not asking about criminals. I'm asking about prisoners of war, and if you could focus your attention on that topic. My question is: The police and the army could give a decision to hold a prisoner of war and that would be a sufficient basis to hold a prisoner of war in the prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But then the Courts had to subsequently adopt a new decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that despite what's written in this report, that the persons were admitted on the basis of decisions issued by the army and the police, in fact, a subsequent decision was required by the Court? That's now your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when the civilian courts would issue a decision, as you now claim, to hold these prisoners, on what basis would they do so, what authority, what basis? What would the decision say?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you could answer it by telling me what the decision said. What would the decision say? This person is being ordered to be held for this reason. And what would the reason be?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was some article of law, now 15 years later you're trying to get me to say which article, which law this was based on. You should put this question to the president of that court or someone who worked in the court. I can't know that. I couldn't tell you off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this question, then. You would agree that prisoners of war that were held at the Knin district prison were still under the authority of the police and the army in the sense that if the police and the army decided to take out the prisoner of war from the prison and exchange that person, for example, they could do that, right, under the law, or do you not know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If an exchange was involved, the Ministry of Justice and Administration would provide us with a letter saying that such and such people would be exchanged and that such and such a person would come to collect them so we would receive all the relevant information from the Ministry of Justice and Administration, information about those who were to be involved in an exchange, such exchanges would have previously been agreed on. I don't know who agreed on them but that was procedure. We would be provided with a list of those individuals and we would be told who was coming to collect those individuals. A bus would arrive of some kind, the bus would take them away, and they would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, maybe you don't know the answer to this question but would you agree that the army had the authority, whether it was done -- how it was done -- I'm talking about the authority, not how it was done -- the army and the police had the authority to take prisoners who were held in the Knin district prison as prisoners of war and take them out and exchange them or release them. They had that authority, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. They didn't have the authority to enter the prison and take individuals out of the prison without the appropriate decision from the district court or from the Minister of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that prisoners of war, once they were put into the Knin district prison, were exclusively under the control of the courts, the civilian courts, and the Minister of Justice, and the army and the police no longer had any authority over them? That's now your -- that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you a document, it's an agreement from the 6th of November 1991, and it's ERN 04247576. There is a translation. You know what? The translation -- the translation may follow the -- I think the first two pages are the B/C/S and the translation are the last two pages. So on the English screen, if you go to page 3. Thank you. Sorry about the confusion. Sir, do you see that this is an agreement that was concluded between the government of Croatia and the JNA on the 6th of November, 1991, and I'm going to draw your attention to point 1 of the agreement. Both sides concur that they will exchange all prisoners or persons deprived of their liberty on the principle of all for all. And point 2 is, the term prisoners shall be held to include all persons deprived of their liberty who are in prisons, detention facilities or prison camps regardless of whether criminal or other any proceedings have been initiated against them." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if -- if you're -- well, let me put this a different way: Doesn't this agreement show that the JNA retained, as the army, retained control and authority over the prisoners of war who were being held in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an agreement. I don't know why you're showing it to me. This is what they agreed on with the Croatian side. This is how things were. That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, how could -- if your testimony is correct, how could the JNA reach this agreement, if it did not have control over the prisoners, if it did not have the authority over the prisoners of war, how could it agree to surrender them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you're asking me something that concerns a higher level. I'm telling you how it worked in our place. When they spoke with the Ministry of Justice there would be an exchange. For example, there was a decision from the Minister of Justice they would say there it would be an exchange on such and such a date and then we would act on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that aside from -- you can tell us only what you observed at the Knin district prison in terms of prison exchanges but you're unable to tell us who had authority over the prisoners of war? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be best to put it this way: Not a single officer at the time could have entered the Knin district prison, nor could he have taken anyone out of that prison. So he had authority of no kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I know you want to answer that question and I know you want to tell the Court that but that's not an answer to my question. My question is about who had authority over those prisoners. And are you -- is that something you don't know? Simply don't know?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do know. In the district prison of court, well it was the president of the district court who had all authority over the prisoners in that prison. He was the only person who had authority over those prisoners, as well as the Minister of Justice and administration of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe we are getting hung up on the word "authority." You would agree with me, would you not, and especially after seeing this document, that the JNA could, on its own authority, its own decision, without asking anybody else, it could exchange prisoners who were being held at the Knin district prison; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they carried out these exchanges. I don't know how they reached agreements or what they agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fine. You don't know. Sir, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you know, don't you, that Milan Martic was involved in proposing prisoner exchanges and talking -- and he spoke publicly about that? You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'm not aware of the fact that he discussed anything of that kind in public or that he was involved in something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 921, please? This is an order dated the 29th of February, 1992. It's a JNA order. And it's entitled, "Stand regarding prisoners" and it says, "In order to establish a more unified manner of treatment of all captured members of paramilitary formations of the Republic of Croatia and to implement a unified criteria on their exchange, the following is ordered." And number 2, it says, "Transfer the captured members of the paramilitary formations of the Republic of Croatia from the collection centres of the Krajina SUP to the military collection centres according to the following. From the Knin SUP to the military collection centre in Knin." Now, were you aware of this order in February of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with anything here. I don't see who this was addressed to. I wasn't in the collection centres. I wasn't anywhere else. I was in the district prison. I can see that this hasn't even been addressed to the district prison. I don't know who drafted this. I don't know who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, my question was very simple. Were you aware of this order? It's yes or no. This long explanation is not required. It's just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me or are you unable to say that this document shows that prisoners of war were being held under the authority of the police, of the Knin SUP?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from the old hospital, the Knin district prison and the JNA barracks, was there any other place in Knin where prisoners of war were held?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, well, I know about the district prison in Knin. I know that there were prisoners there but I don't know about any other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I'm done with that document. I want to talk about how the prisoners were in fact treated. You testified that the prisoners of war at the Knin district prison were kept separate from other prisoners. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many floors the prison had?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one floor was used as a prison. But if you're asking me about the building itself, how many floors there were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, how many floors did the building have?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four. I can't remember exactly. Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And your testimony is that the prisoners were all kept on the same floor?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which floor was this of the three or four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the first floor, and there was the ground floor below that floor. So they were on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So no prisoners were kept on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the first floor. We didn't use the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did you divide up the prisoners of war from the other prisoners? How did you do that? Was there one wing of the building that was used for prisoners of war? Were there certain rooms? How did you divide them up?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a long corridor, and they were on one side. They were all on one floor but not -- we didn't have one room next to another. We had four or five rooms for POWs and four or five rooms for traditional criminals and four or five for those who had been convicted of misdemeanours and who had been sentenced to 30 or 60 days in prison. So these people were Serbs who had carried out misdemeanours so there were these three groups and they were kept separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were all of these rooms on the same hallway?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the same corridor. It's not quite straight but it was the same corridor, one corridor was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, the military part of the prison, the where the prisoners of war were held, that was operated by Sinobad Bosko, wasn't it? He had responsibility for that part, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sinobad Bosko never worked in the district prison, as far as I can remember. He was a member of the military. I know that man. He worked in the factory with me. He was in the military. They had nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He was never present at the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never present in the Knin district prison. He was a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: While you were warden, a number of prisoners died in the prison, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, there are two or three such cases. I can't remember exactly. Two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They died as a result of beatings, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of the prisoners who died in the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does the name Ivan Hodak ring a bell? Died on the 31st of December, 1991 in the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember a man dying on the 31st of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, I know there were two or three individuals who died but I don't know when. I don't know the dates by heart. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, can you please try to refresh your recollection. It was a question concerning one incident, especially on the last day of the year, 1991, and you heard one name. You answered, "I can't remember the names, I can't remember the dates." That was too general, I think. Try to think about that once more and answer that. What was that incident, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that I know that two or three individuals died but as to when this happened, on which date, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I didn't ask you once more about the two or three but about one date, and I didn't want any explanation about maybe not remembering about the cases in general, but to refresh your memory and think about what might have happened at the end of -- on the last day of the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I do know what I did in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, these -- how according to you, did these men die in the prison while you were warden?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which men?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He said he remembered two or three cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned two or three cases of men dying in the prison while you were warden. Do you remember how they died?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the reports, they died of natural causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember the name Mile Skorop? Does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ante Markovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Markovic, if my memory serves me well, was the Prime Minister before the war, if that's the one. But as far as the prison is concerned, that name means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was speaking about the prison. Ivica Radoc?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you can mention all these names but I really can't remember the names of the people who were in the prison. I wasn't interested in names. I was interested in people as people. I didn't attach much importance to the names of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll just ask -- unless Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, I really don't understand your kind of reaction. You were asked about certain deaths and you don't remember names, you say, so you are hearing names. That's a different thing compared to being asked for names. And you cannot answer I think just with, "I don't remember names. I was not interested in names. I was only interested in people." People have names and you received reports which contained names so you might remember these names. It is the case of dead people in the prison of which you were the warden. So it's not very impossible that you remember when being asked certain names. And so you don't have to answer that quickly, just with a sentence, "I don't remember names." That's a little irritating. So this is why I asked you before. Maybe it comes back, the memory, and thinking a little bit, some seconds maybe. Thank you. Mr. Whiting, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll try another name. Davor Tadic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember an inmate -- this is moving on from the inmates who died in the prison. Do you remember an inmate by the name of Ivan Atelj and I may be mispronouncing his name?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Atelj, no, the name means nothing to me, I don't know. I can't -- Q. Well, I'm going to show you a statement that he made and maybe some of his description will bring back -- maybe will refresh your recollection. The statement is -- it's at -- in e-court as 03344210. And if we could turn to page 4 of the English, and page 3 of the B/C/S, please. I have hard copies of the English so... With the assistance of the usher -- but the B/C/S, yes, if we could have page 3 of the B/C/S. You'll see, sir, that this was a statement that was taken on the 3rd of May 1992 at the Zadar police station. The witness doesn't need the English. Sorry, you can look at the screen. It's in your language on the screen. And I draw the Court's attention again to page 4. This individual was arrested in Benkovac on the 14th of October, 1991 and he was held there and then on the 2nd of November, 1991 -- and could we zoom in on the lower half of the B/C/S document? Because it's probably hard for the witness to read it. He was brought to the Knin prison on the 2nd of November 1991, and just -- I'll just go through this on -- it's primarily on page 5 of the English. He -- and just -- I just want you to listen to this, sir, and tell me if you remember this event. Okay? It says that he was brought to the prison and that by 1900 hours he was taken out three times and beaten by boots in his chest, ribs, spine and kidneys. He was told to scrub a 50- metre long corridor. He was kicked while he was doing that. This continued on a daily basis. There were interrogations during which he was beaten severely. He was forced to unload coal from lorries and perform all the worst and most difficult labour, forced to sing. After leaving the prison in Knin, a medical doctor in Zadar established that he had three broken ribs and two vertebrae. Now, if we could turn to the next page in the B/C/S, please? Page 4 of the B/C/S. And zoom in on the top half, please. And he says, he says, "The persons whom Atelj recognised in prison in Knin and their activities, chief prison warden, Kukavica from Karin [phoen], previously employed at Lepoglava. He is trying to conduct his job professionally. Officially prohibits beatings. His opponent is one Plejo, and Jovica Novakovic was Plejo's deputy. While they were in charge of the prison, three prisoners died as a result of beatings. They did not say a word about torture, they allowed beatings of prisoners by civilians, Serbian prisoners, Martic's special force members and all others who wanted to beat them." Now, that's all true, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the Prosecutor is presenting to the witness is not a statement of Ivan Atelj or whatever his name is. This is an official memorandum which is not signed. I should like to ask my learned colleague to tell the witness what the report is, what the report actually is and who is it signed by rather than present it as a statement by this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Counsel is absolutely right. I did say statement and he's absolutely right. It is an official note of an interview with this individual. And that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is the individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The individual is Ivan Atelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But it is signed by somebody, officially in charge, Boro Gambiroza, so to the extent that it is not signed that's not correct, it is signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But it's not signed by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not signed by the interviewee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Your learned colleague takes your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm grateful. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to my question, sir, the things that are written here that Mr. Atelj experienced at the Knin district prison and your role, those things are all true, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not true, Mr. Prosecutor. If I understood you well, when Mr. Atelj was brought in, the warden was Mr. Nikola Kukavica. While here, he describes what the situation was when I was warden. Namely he was still in Croatia and he's saying that I didn't do anything to prevent this kind of thing that is being described here. You must admit that that's a bit far-fetched. It is indeed irresponsible on the part of the person who compiled this note. How could he have known whether I was taking any steps to prevent this, and he knew that before coming to the prison. What was going on in the prison and in which way. That cannot be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, to be clear just so you're not under any misimpression, the information contained in the report purports to be derived from an interview with this inmate. So that's where the information comes from and it's taken after the inmate -- after the prisoner was released. Do you understand that? So it's based on what the prisoner observed at the prison.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he says that he was detained when Mr. Kukavica was the warden but he's talking about the period when I was warden and saying that he knows how I acted. So, please, bear with me, understand what I'm saying. How could he have known what the situation had been like when I was warden and he still had not even been arrested?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, your -- you would agree with me, would you not, that you have testified repeatedly over the course of the past three days, that your memory of dates is not very good and that your memory about when Mr. Kukavica came to the prison was not very certain, was it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, just so it's clear, you deny everything that's written in this report; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't deny it. The man may have experienced all this. What I'm saying is he says that he came to the prison when Mr. Kukavica was the warden, whereas he knows how things were earlier. He was not in the prison when I was there but he knows how things unfolded in the prison at that period when I was. That is just not possible. You can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear, just so you know, so nothing is mysterious here, he was held in the prison for four months. He was released on the 28th of February, 1992. So isn't it possible then that he was in the prison while you were the warden and also while Mr. Kukavica was the warden, since you testified that Mr. Kukavica was a warden for, you thought, perhaps one or two months?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He here says that he recognises some persons in the prison. He refers to the prison warden Kukavica, and he says his predecessor was Plejo, so he refers to the persons that he saw and recognised in the prison, and then he says that I had not undertaken any steps, as if he were some sort of a manager. He has come there to assess whether I took some steps or not. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Plejo. Where does he say that you were Kukavica's predecessor? It may very well be, he says in the B/C/S. We don't have it in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here, "The persons whom Atelj recognised in Knin prison," meaning that he recognised, and it says, "Kukavica from Karin was the warden. He used to work in Lepoglava before that." After that, it says, "A certain Plejo is his predecessor." He says a certain Plejo. He doesn't even know me and Plejo's deputy was Jovica Novakovic. "While they were at the helm of the prison, were beaten to death," and so on and so on. So he doesn't know me. I was working in the central register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just wanted to be clear because then the English is not exactly the same as the B/C/S. I'm looking at the portion that the Prosecutor had read to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter can be of assistance, it says "predecessor" in the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We don't doubt that. It's just that the English doesn't say predecessor. Mr. Milovancevic, you were on your feet, I'm sorry, I was still talking to Judge Hoepfel. Would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, for interrupting you. Can we establish what portion of the English text corresponds to this portion of the B/C/S text? Can my learned colleague the Prosecutor identify that portion so that we can compare?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. It's at the bottom -- it's the last paragraph of page 5, and what appears to have happened is the word -- instead of it saying "predecessor" it says opponent. I think that was a misinterpretation in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I must confess I wondered what the word meant, opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fortunately now it's been cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, how does the learned -- my learned colleague know that this is a mistranslation? How can he know that it is a mistranslation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Precisely because we were just told that because the interpreter just told us that the word and the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor. It's the witness who told you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. We are in a court of law. When the one counsel stands up, the other one must sit down. And that will avoid you addressing each other directly. You talk to each other via the Court and that way you're not going to talk at the same time. I'm not saying anybody specifically. I'm saying both of you. Ask your question, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague, the Prosecutor, said that it was a mistranslation and I should like to ask my learned colleague how does my learned colleague the Prosecutor, who speaks English and does not speak B/C/S, how can he know? How does he know that something is written differently, that something is different in the B/C/S? He can only establish that the English and the Serbian or the B/C/S version are not identical and whether the translation is wrong, he can ask the witness. That is the least that we can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'm lost on the proceedings here. I'm not quite sure where we are now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm really perplexed because both the witness at the interpreter told us that the word is predecessor. I know what sentence was being talked about so I simply said that in the English, it says "opponent" and that's obviously a mistranslation. So I simply inferred that from the information that was provided by the witness and the interpreter. I'm really at a little bit of a loss here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection, Your Honours is to the conclusion of Mr. Whiting that that is obvious mistake or omission. This, he cannot conclude. He can only conclude that things are not identical because the predecessor can also be an opponent to Kukavica. That translation can also be made and it really makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Milovancevic, but is it not so that both the witness, when he was asked by the Bench, and the interpreter, of her own volition, told us that the word predecessor does appear on the B/C/S version and that, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is out of doubt. That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. If we are over that, can we proceed? I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I'm done with this document. Could it be admitted into evidence and given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And I suppose we will get an English translation on the e-court as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that note, wouldn't it be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, it would be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Let's take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, I actually have one more question about this report of the interview of Mr. Atelj. According to this report, Mr. Atelj, was taken to the Knin district prison on the 2nd of November, 1991. Now, you were the warden according to your memory, on that date, correct, on the 2nd of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was on that date but what I do see is that he doesn't recognise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you would focus on my questions. I'll remind you of your prior testimony. Your prior testimony was that you were the warden from August of 1991 and that Mr. Kukavica replaced you for some period of time in 1992, your best memory was March or April of 1992 though you couldn't be certain that he left after some period of time 15 days to two months and then you continued in the position of warden until approximately October or November of 1992. Is that correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The sequence of events is correct, and I don't know about the dates. I have said that I'm not sure. More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you would agree that Mr. Kukavica came in 1992; right? Maybe you don't remember exactly what date but in 1992.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had to be 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So going back to my question, on the 2nd of November, 1991, you were in fact the warden; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. That was really my only question. And now I am, in fact, done with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you, sir, about a few other prisoners, see if you remember them and what happened to them. Do you remember, sir, a prisoner by the name of Ante Kamber, who was held in the Knin district prison from the 27th of December, 1991 to the 6th of June, 1992? Do you remember him, that name, that person?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that person or that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He was regularly beaten by the guards and the only time his treatment improved was when Mr. Kukavica became the warden. Does that help you remember him in any way?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not help me in any way is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about Mr. Zivko Nikolic who was held from the 20th of November, 1991 until the 6th of June, 1992? Do you remember that person, that name?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He was also abused during the entire stay and was only treated well when Mr. Kukavica was the warden. Does that that help you remember him?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about an earlier time, and an inmate named Velibor Bracic who was arrested by Martic's Police on the 15th of June, 1991. He was taken to Golubic where he was detained for two days before being taken to the Knin prison where he was held for a month and physically ill-treated each day. Does that -- do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him personally, but how should I know who arrested him and where they held him? How should I know about that? I don't know anything about that. But I do know him personally because his house is some three or four kilometres away from mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So do I understand your testimony that you do not remember him being held at the Knin district prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the district prison but you asked me who had arrested him and you said that he had been held in Golubic, I believe. How should I know about whether he had been held in Golubic. As for the district prison, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he was ill treated, wasn't he? He was abused at the prison, wasn't he, at the Knin district prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, prisoners at the Knin district prison were regularly beaten and some suffered broken bones, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The SAO Krajina Police were allowed to come into the prison and they beat prisoners there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There was no medical treatment for the injured prisoners, was there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medical treatment was extended to all who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Even the prisoners who had been injured from beatings?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctor came to the prison and anyone who was ill had access to that doctor and there was also a medical nurse, in addition to the doctor, if people needed to be sent to hospital, they would be referred to hospital by the doctor and people went to the hospital and would be escorted there by the guards. Those were the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that include prisoners who had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said all the people in the prison were entitled to medical care. Whether someone had been hit and injured or whoever, in whatever condition, if they required medical assistance they were entitled to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The prisoners were deprived of sleep, they were given inadequate food; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. No one was deprived of sleep, and they were issued meals three times a day, breakfast, lunch and dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They were forced to perform labour while being held at the Knin district prison, isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on several occasions they went out to work, but that was not forced labour, and it was mainly Serbs convicted of misdemeanours who had been in prison for two months and they could in fact hardly wait to go out and work. They requested to go out and work rather than be inside the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said it was mainly Serbs. So do I take it from your answer that it also -- prisoners of war also were taken out to work?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in several cases, I believe. Although they too could hardly wait to get out and they also requested to go out and do some work if there was any work to be had because they would rather go out than stay inside but these were also mainly people but generally it was mostly people convicted of petty offence who had been in prison for 50 or 60 days and these were the people who liked to go out and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, you were the warden of this prison where all of this abuse and mistreatment occurred and you did nothing to stop it. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, do you recall the document shown to you by my learned colleague the Prosecutor, namely the official note referring to Ivan Atelj? It was shown to you a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the English text of that official memo, it is stated that Kukavica was the warden after you, that he respected the law and rules as the warden, and that he was your opponent. In that connection, my question is as follows: Did you violate the house rules in terms of how the detainees or the people in the prison were to be treated? Did you violate them or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I have an objection. The -- obviously the original -- the original is the B/C/S and we have an English translation. And we have an indication at least that the word that opponent has been incorrectly translated. So I'm curious -- so I would object to citing -- referring to that word when the indication is that that is an erroneous translation. And just to press this further the word as I understand it is -- it's [B/C/S/ spoken] in the B/C/S and the translation of that word, I checked it over the break, is predecessor. Whereas "opponent," as I understand it is a different word. So I'm -- I would object to that -- relying on that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as my colleague the Prosecutor founded his work on the official memo and on the statement of Mr. Atelj proceeding precisely from this word opponent which is completely different from the word predecessor or whatever the word is, but this word can really make sense here. I just wanted to check. When we talk about the English variant, can the witness tell us whether he was an opponent to Mr. Kukavica? Namely, did he work differently from Mr. Kukavica? Nothing more. And when my colleague the Prosecutor says that this is a mistake, that it is erroneous, this is something quite different. I want to clarify this from the legal, logical, linguistic aspects and wrap up the subject of the meaning of opponent. I believe that that can be quite logical in this place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say, Mr. Milovancevic, and you are right to the extent that you say it could still be a word that could be used there. However, we got a clarification both from the interpreter and from the witness that the word opponent was never intended to be used. It was intended to be predecessor. And I think if it has been corrected as predecessor, then that settles the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And while we are on the subject, it was bought to my notice during the break that now we have an official translation of -- is it official? You see this one is called unrevised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can clarify that. What's in e-court is the same as what we have in the hard copy. It's the same version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I hear that, Mr. Milovancevic, but if you do want to clear up the question of opponent clearly, just so that maybe nobody makes a mistake later, you can clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in one thing, Mr. Plejo. Did you or did you not abide by the rules that governed how detainees in the district prison in Knin should be treated, whatever the category of prisoners concerned?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did respect those rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we confer about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Sorry about the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, I want to ask you something about the official note in B/C/S. It's the official note about Atelj. In the original text, it says -- well, do you remember that the Prosecutor referred to part of the report and where it says that when he was arrested in November 1991, and then when you were the warden, he was beaten, his ribs were broken, he was forced to do hard labour, he was taken to be interviewed and he was beaten, do you remember that part?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, can you tell us whether that's correct? Did this in fact take place while you were the warden of the district prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such things didn't happen. Apart from in exceptional cases that I have already mentioned. If any excessive acts were committed the perpetrators were punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, were you waiting for us, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it would be rude of me to put questions if -- because the Chamber has the right to confer, of course. I was just waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't hold it against you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not holding it -- we appreciate it and we thank you for it. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as this official note is concerned, the one that concerns Atelj, you saw that it was compiled in the police administration of Zadar, at the beginning of May 1992. Which Ministry of the Interior does the police administration of Zadar belong to?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Croatian MUP probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we exclude the possibility that official notes might be drafted that don't actually reflect the situation in the police?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this report, I would say that this report is not correct. It has been fabricated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to another question put to you by the Prosecution, a question that related to whether any people died in the Knin district prison, well, do you remember the Prosecution asking you a question about that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he showed you some names or rather mentioned some names?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you said that perhaps there were two or three individuals who died?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Judge Hoepfel even drew your attention to the fact that one gains the impression that you are a little cavalier with names, that you don't really pay much attention to them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in response it a question from the Prosecution you said that you couldn't remember any of the names but you did know how you acted in such cases, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Plejo, can you tell us what you as the warden of the Knin district prison did when there it was a death?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the warden of the prison would immediately inform the president of the district court and the Prosecution. That's the first thing he did. I think the president then informed a doctor, someone from the MUP, an inspector, and they would all come to carry out an on-site investigation. They would then draft a report and the final report would be sent to the Ministry of Justice. In such cases, I wanted to know whether the individual had been killed or whether there had been an accident, whether a prison official had committed an error. If the individual hadn't been killed or if a prison official hadn't commit an error, that would mean that the matter had been closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have partially answered the question that I was just going to put to you. In those two or three cases, what did the investigation establish, under what circumstances were these detainees -- or did these detainees die?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was of natural causes, as far as I can remember, heart attacks, all I was interested in was whether we, as prison officials, were responsible for the deaths. If we weren't I wasn't interested in the matter. If we were responsible in such a case, I would certainly have resigned because if a person dies, well, it's not the same thing as if an animal dies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did you want to say when you said, means didn't mean anything for me, what does that statement of yours mean, in fact?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of names. I can't remember the names. At the time, perhaps I knew their names but 15 years have passed since then. I was more interested in how to establish what had actually happened. If they had died of natural causes, of a heart attack or something of that kind, well, that was regrettable but I wasn't responsible, nor were any of the prison officials responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You no longer work in the district prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In other prisons, there are detainees who die, is that the case in other countries, too?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have heard that there have been quite a few such cases and that includes Scheveningen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One more question that relates to a question put to you by the Prosecution, would it be correct to say that you were the prison warden --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe I jumped the gun but the beginning of the formulation looked like a leading question. I accept that maybe I jumped the gun, maybe it was the preamble, but it looked like it was going to be because it was: Would it be correct to say? So I thought it was going to be a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll put the question in such a way that it certainly won't be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, were you the prison warden so that you could make it possible for the police, the army, the citizens, the guards or anyone else could come to the prison and beat and maltreat those people? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I didn't work as warden to enable someone to come and beat the detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was not the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly you asked me whether I was the prison warden in order to allow people to beat the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
