utterances.text: I wasn't there to allow anyone to beat the detainees. I was against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, before I have a couple of other questions let me get back to these deaths you said you remember. Was it two or three cases you remember?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember for sure but it wasn't more than three and it wasn't less than two. I can't remember exactly whether there were two or three cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Then try to remember, please, when was that? What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that people died. I acted in accordance with the law. I would inform the president of the Court. He would arrive with an entire team. I can't remember the names. Believe me. Nor do I know the dates when this took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You are saying now you remember how you called someone in this single incident, do you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases, I know how I acted, but believe me I can't remember the names. 15 years have passed since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You have to tell us what you remember, not any reconstructions of your memory. In which year did that happen, these two or three cases?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly. Perhaps in 1992. I assume that it was in 1992. But I can't claim for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What age were these two or three persons?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know how old they were. You can't expect the prison warden to know when a given detainee was born.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, that is my problem, if I can't get an answer, you know. So please allow me to have my own expectations. So let's change that subject now. You are no prison warden any more today, you said. What do you do at present?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I work as a private businessman. I'm in the transportation business, in the haulier business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: At the time you worked at the Knin prison, were you still in the militia Krajina when you were a warden?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was receiving my salary and I was an official in the Ministry of Justice and Administration. So I received my salary from them. And I had no connection with the militia at that point in time. Later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean you had no connection with the militia at that point in time. Full stop. Later.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was an employee of the district prison and the Ministry of Justice. What did I have to do with the militia later? That's what I wanted to say. There was a list of the employees and you can see my name in that list and you can see the salaries of the various individuals listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And were you still an employee of the factory Tvik [phoen] or when -- if not, when did you stop being an employee of the factory?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 1992. I had to take my work booklet, that was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I don't really understand what this means. I had to take my work booklet. And also was it in the beginning or in the end of this or during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I didn't ask for an exact date.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in mid-1992, I think. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What was in mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You're saying, in mid-1992, I think. But I'm not sure. To what does that refer?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I worked in that factory but when I moved to the Ministry of Justice, I received my salary from the Ministry of Justice. I no longer received my salary from that factory but I still had the possibility of returning there but I took my documents away and handed them over to the archives of the Ministry of Justice and Administration, to the prison, to the Knin district prison. I don't know if there is anything else I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. As a prison warden, did you wear any particular uniform?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually I was in civilian clothes, in a suit of some kind, something like that, but sometimes since everyone was in uniform, you know, most people wore uniforms. Sometimes one would be in uniform, sometimes in a suit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: In what uniform were you when you wore a uniform as a warden of the Knin prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it would be the same kind of uniform that the guards wore. It would be a uniform in two parts, a two-piece uniform. It would be dark blue, a two-piece, dark-blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you give more details?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it resembled a suit, the uniform resembled a suit. It was like a police uniform. But the police uniform was a light blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: There are certain insignia on a uniform usually or other particulars.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were insignia but I didn't have any insignia. There were no insignia -- there were no insignias for me to wear. Usually a warden should be in civilian clothes but since it was war, everyone wore a uniform, so one felt a little awkward wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Right now I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Did Mr. Martic, Milan Martic ever visit the prison in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Milan Martic never visited the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether all prisoners of war who were captured by the SAO Krajina or the RSK forces were kept in ordinary prison or, if not, how was a distinction made in which place to put a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, they were kept in the Knin district prison, which is where all the other prisoners were kept but they were in another section. They were all on one floor, in the same premises, four or five rooms would be used for one group of prisoners. Other rooms for others. They were all there together but they weren't all in the same rooms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm also asking how did you make the determination, on what bases, as to where to put them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, naturally you can't put a POW together with a Serbian who killed some other Serbian. You can't have them in the same room so -- they had to be separated. You can't put someone who was guilty of having committed a misdemeanour together with someone who had murdered an individual. So there were these rules, the POWs were held together and these others were in two groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you -- my apologies are in order. Now, there was a report on the district prison in Knin which was written by you, and according to that report, those persons convicted for violation of military discipline were also detained at the Knin district prison. What sort of breaches of military discipline resulted in persons being detained in that prison? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's similar to a misdemeanour. There could have been misdemeanours committed for which you have a sentence up to 30 days in prison but I don't know exactly what they were guilty of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What type of misdemeanours?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of misdemeanours. I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the disciplinary measures that would be taken against prison employees. You recall? What I want you to tell me: What circumstances would determine whether a person would be reinstated after dismissal or brought back to work? Are you understanding me? When -- that person, you having taken the decision that he was guilty of a breach of discipline and that it warranted in the circumstances a dismissal, what would be the circumstances that would make you decide, okay, we are going to take him back and put him back on the work that he was doing or put him back within the prison? When?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would very reluctantly return a such a person o to work but if the warden is replaced or if there is insufficient staff then perhaps the person would be returned because we didn't have sufficient number of trained staff. So that could be a reason. But otherwise, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, was there an instance that you spoke of where the person was dismissed and then returned to work? What were the circumstances there that provoked you to allow that person to return?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't allow that to happen. I think that some other warden reinstated him and I assume he did so because we only had 19 employees who had been trained to work in prisons. So that was probably the reason for which this other warden reinstated him, but there were probably some conditions that had to be met. I assume that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that sometimes you would bend the rules because you were short staffed, but on reinstatement you would apply conditions as a sort of safeguard hopefully for the future? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that I dismissed that individual. I would never have returned him to work. I would rather have taken in some younger man, even if he hadn't been trained. He would have learned how to perform his duties. But some other person might have thought differently. How am I to know what was in his mind when he acted in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I'm going to ask you now about women or female inmates, and during the time that you spoke about, how many female inmates did you see?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few. They were mostly men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When you say a few, under ten?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite sure it was under ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And where were they housed? Where were they kept normally?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were separated and there were a few cases of females staying very -- for a very, very short period but generally speaking they were separated. It would not be logical to have them together with the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And where in the prison would they be, which floor, which room?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think that they were in a separate room, one room at the end of the corridor, but they stayed for a very brief time. I don't know even whether a couple of women only stayed in the prison overnight. I'm not quite sure. And there were no women POWs. There were Serb women there for different reasons, but only a very few cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What would those Serb women have been there for if not POWs?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were probably -- they were involved in some petty offence or something. Wasn't some grave crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In respect of the female prisoners, did you have female prison officers?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have female guards. We didn't have a single woman who was trained as a guard at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I want to ask you this question: You remember in response to Mr. Whiting, the learned counsel for the Prosecution, you said that two or three prisoners died. How would the cause of death of a particular prisoner who had died be determined by you at the time? You had spoken as to natural causes.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I have already explained. A physician would come, a judge, a Prosecutor, an inspector from the SUP. They would all come at the same time to establish the situation and then they would submit a report to the Minister of Justice. And the Minister of Justice would then report to me or, rather, I would seek information from him as to whether it was a natural cause of death or an error on the part of the prison staff, but in no instance it was a mistake on the part of the prison staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Let me ask: Did you first give the information about such a death to the Prosecution or to the ministry, or to both, the first information you gave, the first notice?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our obligation to immediately inform the president of the district court in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about your obligations but about what you did.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well specifically, the president of the district court, and he would then undertake the other necessary steps, the investigation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: When would the ministry, the minister, learn?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my obligation to inform the minister. I may have also informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I did not ask you about your obligations but about what you did just as before, and can you -- do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to help. Just listen a little bit. I think what the judge wants to know is how -- what made the physician, the minister, the member of the SUP and the prosecutor come? Obviously they don't know about the death. This person dies in your prison. So for them to come, some report must be given to them. Now, that's -- it is that first report to them, that reports the death, that the judge is asking you about. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. That report. And that was sent to whom? Once more, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a person died in the prison, it was my duty to immediately inform the president of the district court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, please answer my question. What happened on the ground? To whom did you make, send the first report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what I am saying. If I understand you well, whom did I inform? I informed the president of the district court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That is not what you were saying. You were telling me something about your duties but I was asking you what you then said -- yeah, just --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just wait, please. At what time did the minister learn from you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would inform the ministry immediately, if not during working hours, it would be on the next day but what I had to do immediately was to inform the president of the district court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And you mean you would inform the minister also immediately or first the Court?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First the Court. That being my obligation. And later, I could also inform the minister, but first the Court had to be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean by "first" and "later"? What time you -- did you inform the minister? Was that after the full investigation had taken place, together with the results of this investigation, or was it a preliminary report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have said that it wasn't my obligation to inform the minister. But if I talk to him or had dealings with him I would inform him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please, Witness, answer my questions. What do you mean now when you talked with him, you mean at the occasion of a contact you may have then mentioned also such an event? Do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it wasn't exactly the same when you mentioned it earlier, not answering my question, that you informed immediately the Court and the minister, was it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Perhaps we didn't understand each other properly. I repeat: It was my obligation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's fine. Now, you also were talking of nights. That made me then think I would ask you something more. How about the nights? Did you or were you ever on duty overnight?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You mean never?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have come. I would come in for tours, but to be on duty, that would presuppose spending the entire night there. I didn't do that but I would come on occasion, sometimes twice also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So tell me a little more or -- what kind of occasions were that for you to come to the prisons during the night?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, if I was in the vicinity of the prison, I would go in and see, even if there was no particular reason. If I was passing by the prison, I would certainly stop and go and see what was happening in the prison. And that happened many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Where was your home at this time? How far from the prison was it, just --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some eight to nine kilometres far from the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But it happened often that you were in the vicinity during the night, I mean?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that was the city, downtown. I lived on the outskirts, in the village, and of course I would come downtown and that's why I would be passing by. I was a young man, a lad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: How old were you at that time? In your late 20s or something? Is that right? In 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I was 28 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the guards, did they also live some -- at some places far away or did they have a house all together where they lived? What was their accommodation like?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some lived far, even farther away than me. Some lived nearer. That depended on the particular guard. Some had rented flats in Knin. Most of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was everything. Sorry to take so much of your time. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Not at all. Do you have any more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Hoepfel, for that kind intervention. Now, how would the prison be cleaned, kept clean? Was there a system in place for cleaning and who would clean?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have a cleaning lady. The detainees did the cleaning. There were some rules as to how a bed should be made, how a room should be kept clean, and they would take turns cleaning the corridor or one room would be cleaned one day and then the next day the second room. But everyone had to keep their rooms tidy. If there were five of them in a room, they would agree between them how to do it but the room had to be kept in order and tidy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Did they also have to clean the toilets which they used?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, there were, were there not, officers with dormitories on the premises or quarters on the premise, whilst you were there? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in these other section, there were some who lived far and because of that, they could spend nights there, but there were -- there was no one who was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. They would spend nights there and where specifically on the building would that be? On the ground floor? On the first floor? Which wing? You could tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were in the same wing, on the top floor of the building, I believe, in a section of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, there again, would the prisoners also clean there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honours. No, because that would mean that they would have to go out of the prison, and that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So are you saying that they would never go out of the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only into the compound for walks. We had organised half- hour walks during the day, in the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Did you ever know Captain Dragan or his men being in the prison compound or the dormitory or quarters there on the premises?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, was there a guard room on the premises? A duty guard room?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There was a room. It was the shift leader's room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And where was it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was some place in the middle of the prison, in the centre of the prison, and one of the rooms was assigned to be the shift leader's room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And would prisoners clean that room?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I suppose that they would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could you tell me where room number 1 would have been? And where it was located? And if you're able to say how many beds would have been in there and how many prisoners it would have accommodated? I'm sorry to ask you a compound question. My -- I'm sorry to ask you a compound question. Let me just break it down for you. Let me stick first of all to room number 1. And I start off with where it was located so as not to confuse you.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from memory, Your Honours. I don't remember where the numbers were, on which side. I really cannot remember now where the serial numbers started, whether it was on the right or on the left side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Let me put it another way or ask you slightly differently. Which was the smallest room for the housing of prisoners, roughly what size it was and how many prisoners did it accommodate?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the smallest room was about 15 or 20 square metres in area. That was the smallest one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm coming up to my last two questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The question also was and how many prisoners did it accommodate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Judge Hoepfel.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have replied to that earlier. Namely, eight cubic metres were the required space per inmate. So if the room was smaller, we would put a fewer inmates in it, in order to avoid overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just a simple question. How many people were accommodated in this 15 square room, smallest room. Just answer that. We want you to go home this weekend. Don't you want to go home?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps four or five detainees would be in this smallest room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm one of the old persons you spoke about so I can't work out maths at this stage but let me go on. Where was the food you ate yourself and you gave to the prisoners prepared? I think that was your evidence, that the prison officers and the inmates ate the same food, if I recall rightly. Isn't that your evidence? And I want to know where it was --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Initially, I went to the army and I requested them to give us food. We had to give them the head count and we would eat the same food, the prison staff, the guards, and the detainees. I specifically ate at home because I would get my food from home. The shift guards, they would eat their food, they have their meals in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Do you know of any cases of food poisoning in relation to inmates or anybody associated with the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this officer on duty, the shift leader, had to taste the food first, and we never had any cases of food poisoning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And this now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe the sense of your question is illnesses coming from the food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Food poisoning may be a misunderstanding expression. It sounded like the danger of someone putting poison to the food. So someone had to taste first and so on. This is I think -- that was not the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I don't know if there was something missing in my communication to the translators, interpreters, but what I really meant is the after-effect of taking the food because something is wrong with the food instead, not interference with the food by third parties, to place something in it that is poisonous. Would you like to answer that question again, then? Were there any cases of inmates getting food poisoning from bad food?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That never happened. It was the same food, and it would be eaten by the guards and by the prisoners, and this never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My last question to you now, sir: Was there a locksmith shop there? Or any type of iron mongering? Was there a locksmith shop at the prison, at any time whilst you were there? You know what I mean by locksmith?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. There was no -- nothing of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Or anywhere that was like an iron foundry or iron work?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honours, we didn't have any such workshops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Can I just ask you, Mr. Plejo, to please listen very carefully to my questions and answer directly to my questions so that you can go home this weekend. Otherwise you're going to stay here if we don't finish with you. Let me just start with some of the questions that you were asked by Judge Nosworthy. I just want to develop them a little bit before I go to my questions. You said you gave the army a head count and they gave you the food to eat. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the army also supply you with food for civilian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It supplied us with food for everybody. Actually we would go fetch the food from them with our own vehicle, the food which they would give us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before the SAO Krajina was established, before you had prisoners of war, where did you get the food for your civilian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, before that, the prison was not in existence. I have told you that prior to the eruption of these conflicts, there had been no prison in Knin and I described how this prison came into existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also said that when somebody died in the prison, you would mention it to the minister when you met him. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that how you gave reports of deaths to the minister? You would mention it when you met him? And if you didn't meet him, you didn't mention it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I said was, it was my obligation to inform the Court. After the on-site investigation, the Court would draw up a report and submit it to the minister and the minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you're going to please listen to my question. You are being asked about the first report, when you notified the minister about the death so that the minister can come and do his investigation and then give you a report and then you can do what you -- that is the first, when you report the death. You said when you met the minister, you would tell him. I'm asking you a very simple question. Is that how you reported deaths to the minister, as and when you met him?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the minister was not in charge of the investigation. The Court was in charge of it. I didn't have to inform him. He would receive the results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Who did you report to when a person -- when a person dies, what did you do? What happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I informed the president of the Court. The president of the district court. And they would come and conduct an on- site investigation. The Court representative, the prosecutor's office and the doctor would come and establish the cause of death and they would be the ones submitting a document to the minister to explain what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Plejo. We are going to take a short break. We'll come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks for the answer you gave me before we went out for the break. Can I just ask: You mentioned at some stage that if it happened that the person died at night or outside working hours, you would report the death the following day. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The head of the guard shift would then inform the duty judge, the investigative judge, and he would then act on the information, but an on-site investigation would be carried out immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were also asked by -- okay, before I come to that, in your testimony in chief you mentioned that there were two lavatories in that building. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did they stay being two for the entire period that the building was being used as a prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we moved into another part of the prison, more room was taken. We had more room and there was a lavatory that was made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many lavatories did you have when you were using the building as a prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large facility and there were three or four toilets there. I don't know exactly how many. I think there were three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the maximum number, if you can remember, and I'm not asking to you give a specific number just an approximation, what's the maximum number of prisoners you held at any one time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, as far as the facilities are concerned, there could have been up to 100 of them but there were never that many. There were never more than 50 or 60. That was the maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, which one is more nearer the correct number, you said there could have been up to 100 of them but there were never more than 50 or 60. Is it 100 or 50 or 60? What are you telling me?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that the maximum number was between 50 and 60 but as far as the facility is concerned, the facility was large enough to provide accommodation for 100 individuals. But we never had that many detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And the lavatory facilities, what capacity did they have? I don't know how to put this question. How many individual facilities were there inside each lavatory, more or less?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think four to five people could have used the toilet at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, four to five people, three to four lavatories, that's about 20, and you had a maximum at any one time of about 60 people there.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these four to five lavatories included the female facilities as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one separate toilet so the women would go there, but while I was the warden, I don't think there was a single woman there. There were very few of them. But there was one toilet for women. Naturally we had one toilet that was to be used by women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me get your answer quite clear. When you say there were about four or five lavatories, do you include the women's facility or when you say there was a separate one for ladies, is that in addition to the four or five?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a separate toilet for women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand it was separate. All I want to know is, is it part of the four or five or is it additional to the four or five?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just said, there were four or five toilets for men and there was one separate toilet for women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes it slightly clearer so in total there would have been five or six toilets?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if I can just get to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask for clarification as there is always confusion about the vocabulary, washrooms, toilets, lavatories, bathroom, was a question yesterday or the day before, as you -- if there were washrooms, like for showers or for other washing facilities, did you include that when you talked of lavatories or is that an extra institution?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some showers next to these facilities, but these facilities were separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. A little earlier, when Judge Hoepfel was asking you questions and he said -- you said, "Well, I worked in that factory but when I moved to the Ministry of Justice I received my salary from the Ministry of Justice. I no longer received my salary from that factory but I still had the possibility of returning there but I took my documents away and handed them over to the archives of the Ministry of Justice and Administration, to the prison, to the Knin district prison. I don't know if there is anything else I can say." Remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That answer was I think in response to a question that related to what you did when you left the factory. Now, when you testified in chief, you indicated that while you were working at that factory, at the invitation of Mr. Martic, you became a reserve policeman. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, and then you said while you were doing that job of a police reserve policeman, you were called to Golubic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And then while you were at Golubic, you then went to -- and you worked for the SAO Krajina SUP when you were in Golubic, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that as part of the reserve force, I was in Golubici. I was a member of the reserve force and then I received a summons to go to Golubici. I think I have already explained that. I don't think I could explain it better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like you to explain it better because it is not quite clear. To my mind it appeared as if when Mr. Martic invited you to become a reserve policeman, that was one job that you did after- hours when you knock off from the factory, okay? And then that while you were doing that job, you then got summoned to Golubic and you were running training programmes at Udbina which wouldn't allow to be on duty at the factory. So I got the impression that you were employed now while you were at Golubic by the institution at Golubic and no more by the factory. Was that impression wrong?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you're part of the reserve force, then you can remain there and you are still employed by the factory but you don't go to work in the factory. Those were the rules. So I didn't go to work in the factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What I do -- maybe let me just ask you this question. So when you were now called to Golubic, you were still called to Golubic in your capacity as a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And yet you spent your entire day at Golubic this time. You didn't do work after hours like you did when you were still a traffic controller?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to work in the factory while I was part of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me get you clear again. Are you saying from the time that Mr. Martic invited you to become a reserve policeman and you controlled traffic, you didn't have to report to the factory at all? You were now full-time traffic officer and full-time police reservist and doing that but the factory was still paying you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That clears the picture a little bit. So that even when you left traffic control and you were now stationed at Golubic, you were still being paid by the factory?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Those were the rules. Those had been the rules since 1945 so I received my salary from the factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. Just answer my question. I just want to understand the picture. Okay. That clears -- in fact, it cuts across a number of questions I was going to ask. That is very helpful. You also mentioned in your evidence-in-chief that -- okay -- you said you had ten or so captured men but you have told us today that the maximum number you had at any one time was 50 or 60, but at the time you mentioned having ten or so captured men, you said you had something like 15 to 20 men who secured the building. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying that at that time you had 15 or 20 men guarding 10 captured people?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But, Your Honours, some were at home. They didn't all have to be working their shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified that at some stage, plus/minus 15 or 20 days after these men had been got secure in the prison, these men, these very 15 to 20 men, left the Territorial Defence force. You remember that? And when they did, they also -- oh, yeah, they left the Territorial Defence force. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left, I don't know where they went. I assume they didn't leave the Territorial Defence force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. You said when the Territorial Defence force left, plus minus 15 or 20 days later, when they left the hospital, in other words, the impression I got was that these men who were securing the prison were not at the hospital for a long time. They were there for plus minus 15 to 20 days. Was I right to -- did I hear you well?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about 15 days. They left when professional guards took up their positions. So the men rotated. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Now, you also mentioned that the prison, the district prison, was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice and Administration and that it was never under the Ministry of Interior. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. My question to you is: Do you know whether the Ministry of Interior had any authority over any other prisons at all? Not necessarily Knin. Any others.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think so. I know about three prisons. The Minister of Justice had authority over those prisons and I doubt he would have allowed someone else to meddle with his work. I have Mr. Matkovic in mind who was in that position at the time. As to whether the police had a prison of their own in some other town, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm a little confused by your answer. This is the problem with long answers. You said first, "Your Honours, I don't think so. I know about three prisons. The Minister of Justice had authority over those prisons and I doubt he would have allowed someone else to meddle with his work." That's the one thing. Now you say, "As to whether the police had a prison of their own in some other prison, I really don't know." I'm not asking you whether the police had a prison of their own, I want to know if, to your knowledge, the police had authority over any other prison, other than the Knin prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Could we have Exhibit 919 on the screen, please? The problem I'm going to have with that exhibit is that I may not be able to give you the B/C/S reference. Oh, it is pages -- I'm going to be looking at pages 11 and 12 in the B/C/S, okay? Now, in the English, I'm looking at pages 29, 30 and 31. Are we on the same page? Metaphorically speaking? Let's start with page 29. On page 29, if you can look at the prisoner numbered 69.H, Vinko Milic, do you see that man?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have it on the screen, Your Honour. Mirko? What was the name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, Vinko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I can be of assistance. Here we have the first column with the numbers of the detainees. We have detainees from number 200 -- no, perhaps it's appeared now. No it's there now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 11 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Here, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the screen now. I apologise, Your Honours. I wanted to be of assistance. The number was 200 and something. I wanted to help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, do you see number 69.H?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see his name is Vinko Milic? I hope I'm pronouncing it correctly. Witness, do you see his name?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Now, look at the penultimate column to the right, where reasons for release are being given. They say there that he was released following the verbal order by Nikola Amanovic. Now, who was Nikola Amanovic? Do you know him.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour. I really don't know who he is and how this could have been done on his verbal order. This was at the very beginning. Perhaps it was from the Court. Perhaps he used the phone to inform us. Sometimes the Court would say, "Release such and such a person, we have a statement of reasons," but I don't know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I seem to remember that -- I may be wrong -- there may be evidence to say that Nikola Amanovic was Mr. Martic's deputy. Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard that that man was his deputy. I don't know the man. It was at the very beginning. It was the 10th of September, 1991. I can't remember how this could have been done on a verbal order, unless someone said that a decision would subsequently be provided of the perhaps someone phoned up and said, "We are drafting a decision." I assume that's how things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will finish quickly if you can stick to the questions. Maybe something was to follow but whether something was to follow or not is immaterial. What is material here is that the person giving the order is Nikola Amanovic. And if something follows it will probably follow from him but he's the one giving the order and --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, if his name is written down here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Look at the prisoner -- I don't know when I suppose it must be still on the same page, number 62.S, Zeljko Milijas. Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milijas, just a minute, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now look at the same column that gives the reason for release, order by the Territorial Defence chief. You see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you see the next one below him, number 63.S, Jandrija Zezelj, also the same order, Territorial Defence force?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the next one, 64.S, Djuro Kolundzic same order.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you turn to page 12 of the B/C/S, which is page 31 of the English version, look at prisoner number 76.H, Ante Hercegovac, you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it in this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Number 76.H. Ante Hercegovac.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can see that? That he was released as per the order by Milan Martic. You see that order? And handed over to the JNA. You see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you look at the one above him, 75.H, Miro Pavic, you see that he was exchanged -- okay. You say the exchanging was done by the court. I beg your pardon I'm sorry. But look at number 73.H, again another verbal order from Nikola Amanovic. You see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at prisoner number 130.H. I'm not quite sure what page it will be. It's on page 40 of the English translation. I'm not quite sure what page it will be in the B/C/S. Have we got the B/C/S? That's prisoner number 130.H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's page 15 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 15 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you see there that the reason for his release is as per the order of the Minister of the Interior, deputy, Amanovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you look at number 133.H, Igor Radosevic. It's per the order by the minister, let's go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Minister of Interior, Amanovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think we have shown quite a lot of examples now. You see that these are people who are said to have been released by the order of this ministry, which according to your testimony, did not have any authority over the prison. This is rather surprising.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you what I think happened. This is when the district prison was being established. It was in September when the district prison was established, they didn't have any decisions on detentions. We probably requested that people be placed in detention or that they be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991. This was immediately after the establishment of the Knin district prison. We probably requested from the MUP that either criminal reports should be filed against these people or that they should be set free. So that was the reason. Those were the first few days, that was perhaps the first month, during which this prison exists. We had to wait for the list to arrive from the Ministry of Justice to the Ministry of the Interior. Two or three months later the situation changed. So it was a period during which we wanted to have a decision for all of those who were detained. We wanted criminal reports, criminal proceedings to be instituted against individuals or we wanted them to be released but we wanted to have decisions stating the reasons for which they were pr in prison. Perhaps there was no reason to prosecute these individuals and the deputy minister therefore ordered that they should be set free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, we don't have much time and you are again -- your elaborate answers just bring tonnes and tonnes of questions that one could ask. For starters, why would you ask the MUP -- you say, "We probably requested from the MUP that either criminal reports should be filed against these people or that they should be set free." Why would you ask them if they didn't have any authority? They are -- they are in your custody, you charge them or you release them. Now, I don't want to go into that. All I'm saying is -- all I want to find out from you is, are you now conceding that at least at sometime, the Ministry of the Interior had authority on the people who were detained in the Knin prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you accept that as a concession -- or as an admission, rather?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, earlier on I tried to explain this. We said that in Golubic there were some people who were detained they were transferred to Knin and when this was done the Ministry of the Interior arrested them. They to issue a decision or to file a criminal report and submit it to the Court so that they would continue with the criminal proceedings or so that they would release these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. -- just don't keep repeating the same answer. We are sufficiently --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now, listen to my question. If word will to come from the Minister of the Interior on whether or not people must be charged or released, then they had authority over those people, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the district prison was established, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not saying before. I'm saying when that happened, whenever it happened, then it means they had authority, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, you don't need any explanation. Just hold it there. Please let's not waste time. Let's answers the questions as they are put and just the questions as they are put. This, therefore, is not in accordance with what you told us, that the Minister of the Interior never had any authority over the people.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you haven't understood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well if I misunderstood you that's fine just say no, then, but if I'm correct, say yes.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police arrested individuals and had the right to detain them for 72 hours and then a criminal report would be submitted to the Ministry of Justice. I have to explain this so there is no way for me to explain this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I abandon that question and I a abandon that question. Don't worry. I think I've got enough on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask who was that inspector Milivoj Bjelja, who is that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was an inspector, he was probably someone from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to English page 44? It is prisoner number 161.H, and in B/C/S, I don't know which page. The penultimate column says, "Released as per verbal order by inspector Milivoj Bjelja." This is what I was referring to. And that was in October, wasn't it, of 1991? Is that true? Is that correct? Do I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably correct, since that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to go to the first page of this document. Okay. Fine. Now, you said a little earlier, sir, that this may have happened at the time when you were still beginning and you didn't have your systems in place. When did you have everything in place so as to exclude the authority of the Ministry of the Interior? Now, when you said now from today onwards the prisons are strictly under the Department of Justice, Department of Justice only, when was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't provide you with a precise date but two or three months later, everything had been set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Give me an estimate, sir.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps two, two and a half months later, everything fell in place. Then it was only the district court that issued decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Two and a half months later than what? Give me an approximate date, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two and a half months after mid-August, when the district prison was actually established. So two and a half months later. You can't establish everything or put everything into place on the very first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: August or September -- August of -- August of 1991, rather, sorry.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of mid-August, when the district prison was formed, so two and a half months after its establishment, we needed time to establish everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is August 1991, right. Fine. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that will take us to August, September, October, somewhere in the middle of November. Okay. Where are those pages of mine? We'll leave that topic. Now, in November of 1991, were there bars installed on the windows of the old hospital?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we installed bars but, you know, we didn't have any money so as the money came in, we would install the bars. We didn't install bars on all the windows at the same time but we did install bars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question now? In November of 1991, had you installed bars on the windows of the old hospital?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps there were several windows that didn't have any bars at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you had installed some.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who installed these bars?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a factory that produced the bars. I think it was called Tehno Metal. They did such work so they installed the bars. It was a factory from Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And why were these bars installed?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To prevent people from escaping. That's what prisons were like. That's how we operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Did at any stage -- did the left wing of the old hospital ever be used as part of the prison at any stage?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And also the right wing?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right wing was used only initially because we only had a small number of rooms, three or four rooms, but when we started using the left wing we no longer used the right wing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did we hear you correctly to say -- let me ask you this question very clearly: Who brought prisoners -- I'm thinking here only of prisoners of war -- to the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I think also you've also indicated that the institution at Golubic also did bring some.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was the first group. They arrested them somewhere, they had no place where to keep them, so they brought just this first group that we discussed a couple of days ago. So the very first people who came there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The first ten who were guarded by the 15 to 20 men?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying that after that, no other prisoner came there from Golubic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, but I suppose not. After the prison was formed there, they were kept in Golubic because there was no other place where they could be kept but once the prison was in place they would be brought to prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You confuse me. When you say you don't know, after you've just said to me Golubic brought only the first ten, I don't know what to accept as the correct story now. Is it the ten only or is there a possibility that others were brought after the ten?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my office was in the prison compound. From where people were brought later, I don't know. They may have been brought from there or not. I had no way of knowing. What was important for me when they were brought to the gate was that they had a relevant decision for detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, listen. I think it's obvious to all of us that anybody who gets brought to a prison is brought for a good reason, and if a person is brought by -- you got to know which police station arrested him. If it's a civil police, why they arrested him and there must be some documentation. You just don't accept people in the prison, they don't just give you a human being and go away, don't I?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I have been saying, Your Honour. I was interested in the document. Who arrested him, what the person's name was, but where they were arrested, was it in the north or in the south or west, what I wanted to know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know what? You have testified today that some people have been brought -- were brought there from Golubic. How did you know they came from Golubic? You have told of people being transferred from Golubic. You know, I have this clear recollection. I just can't get the page now. Didn't you say so today?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say. Your Honours, I was in Golubic and I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not saying you said you were in Golubic. I'm saying you have told us today that prisoners were transferred from Golubic while you were the warden there at the prison. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. I'm sorry if it is not correct. Now, did the JNA have detention facilities at their barracks? Do you know.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours. I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you testified today that the International Committee of the Red Cross had lists of prisoners and therefore no prisoner could be hidden away from them. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they would come to the prison and they wanted to see the POWs' number and they would be immediately submitted lists, and later they would come and visit those people all the time. We had no reason to hide the lists of POWs from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question? Where did they get the lists from? Just give me where they got the lists from, without any explanation.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave them the lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So if indeed there was an intention to hide some prisoners, those who were intended to be hidden would not be mentioned on the list. I'm saying "if." It's a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, but this was just this one single prison and if one were to hide somebody, then the other detainee would tell the ICRC people that that was the case. It was impossible in a word to hide anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question. It's a hypothetical question. I'm asking you a question. If there is an intention to hide, just any person who is to be hidden would not be put on the list, because the ICRC gets the list from the very people whom they are coming to inspect. That's -- that could happen.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything is possible, but there was no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The two or three prisoners that you remembered dying of natural causes in prison, are you able to remember their names?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That concludes my questions. Any questions, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the questions asked by Their Honours in relation to the hygienic and sanitary conditions, the times of baths and the dispensing of meals, were there any rules that regulated such issues?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the rules?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the house rules, the house regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you implement those rules?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the rules regulate the obligation of the warden of the district prison to be on duty at night? Did it stipulate that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Hoepfel asked you what you were currently pursuing, what job you were currently doing. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were a haulier?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And where are you a haulier?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why aren't you a haulier in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I've been banished from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you -- why don't you go back there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I would go hungry. I wouldn't have a place where I could work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And that concludes my questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic? Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Plejo, Judge Nosworthy asked you at page 49 whether all of the prisoners of war were kept in an ordinary prison and then you answered that they were kept in the Knin district prison. I have two questions about that. The first is: Are you aware that prisoners of war were also kept in other prisons in the Krajina, such as the Glina prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Glina, too, as part of the prison, yes, they were kept there also, I believe, but I never went to that prison so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's sufficient. I just -- my second question is: In respect of Knin district prison being an ordinary prison, while you were warden, was there ever any time where the military had authority over a part of the Knin district prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you answered at page 80 to a question that -- in response to a question about -- well, let me just follow up on that last question because I think I put it unclearly. I said where the military had authority over a part of the Knin district prison. Let me put it a little more broadly. Did the military ever, when you were warden have authority over a part of the building, that is the old hospital building?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over this part where we were, this one floor which we had occupied, the army could not go in there, nor use it in any way. I believe they did use a room in the basement in one part of the building. I believe that the name was supplementary battalion or something like that but they had no connection with us whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that the -- they actually kept prisoners in one part of the building, over which you had no authority, but they kept prisoners of war in a part of the building? Isn't that in fact the case?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went into their section and I never allowed them to enter our part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is the answer that you don't know what they were doing in that part of the building?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the army was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going -- at page 80, you were asked who brought prisoners of war to the prison and your answer was "Mainly the army." It's true, isn't it, that the police also brought prisoners of war to the prison; correct? The police of the SAO Krajina and the RSK.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, the army would sometimes surrender them to the police. The police would take them to the investigating magistrate, and then they would then take them -- bring them to us so there was no rule actually. They could have been brought by both the police or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, there were times when the police brought prisoners of war to the prison?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some instances of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look just one last time at Exhibit 919, please, and if we could look at page 7 of the B/C/S and page 18 of the English, and I'm looking -- I want to look specifically at number 197, Milan Dukic. It's the next-to-last one there. Is the English up yet? Milan Dukic there, 197. He was according to this document, arrested on the 18th of October, 1991 and released on the 22nd of November, 1991, released as per decision by the Knin SJS which is a reference to the Knin police; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is an abbreviation which indicates the Knin police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't think that SJS refers to public security station or the police?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it refers to. I'm not familiar with that abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If it does, let's just assume for a moment that it does refer to that, would you accept that this indicates that even by the 22nd of November, 1991, things were not fully set up, as you were saying, that it was still not fully set up and that the police still had some authority as of that date in the prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police could not have had any authority. This is specific case, according to a specific decision, and I have no way of knowing what the specific case is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what I'm referring to is that you gave an estimate of how long it took to set up the prison and you said two and a half months after August, and in a long discussion with His Honour Judge Moloto you finally concluded that it was probably by November. Would this indicate to you that by -- that by November 22nd, 1991, still not fully set up; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the police could remand someone in custody for a maximum of 72 hours. Possibly this was the decision which is in question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know in the specific instance. If I had a case file in front of me I would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I won't pursue it. Finally, you were asked about inmates, about food poisoning or I'll say more broadly, inmates, detainees getting sick from food as a result of eating food. And you testified -- it's at page 61 -- your answer about whether that ever happened was no, that never happened. Now, my question is this: Over these past it two and a half days there has been -- there have been so many things that you're unable to remember from that time period, how is it that you're able to say with certainty, no, that never happened, with respect to food poisoning?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the same meals were eaten by the guards and the people deprived of liberty, and that is one incident that I would certainly have remembered because I would have problems with the staff also. It is impossible for me not no remember a thing like that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But if it happened, let's suppose that it happened that only a detainee got sick from the food, then you wouldn't necessarily know about that or remember that, would you, if it was just the detainee and not the staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PLEJO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it was just one case, I wouldn't perhaps remember whether it was a detainee or a prison staff member, but if there was a poisoning, it would probably have involved more people and the prison staff, including the prison staff and the detainees. It is next to impossible for just one person to have food poisoning and the rest not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
